The app can tell you which keys it answers to. Press **⇧?** and the list is there — grouped, and filtered to the screen you are actually on, so Settings shows only the keys that work in Settings and the replay workbench adds the ones that only work over a recording.

It could not do that before, and the reason is worth saying: there was no list. Nine chords had grown up across five files — a React hook, two bare keydown listeners, an onKeyDown on a slider, and Rust — and working out what the app responded to meant reading all five. Three of those paths did not share the rule that a shortcut must not fire while you are typing into a field. A cheat sheet written by hand would have fixed the visible half and left the real one, because a hand-written list is a second copy of the keymap and the copy starts lying the first time a key moves. So the keys live in one table now, and the sheet is generated from it. If a key is not in the table it does not appear; if it moves, the sheet moves with it.

New keys. **⌘,** opens Settings from any window, including Settings' own. **⌘1**, **⌘2** and **⌘3** go to the home screen, the library, and the recording you already have open. **⌘B** puts the sidebar away and gives the room back — and gives it back at the width you had dragged it to, not squeezed down to a sliver you then have to aim at. **⌘R** starts a meeting; **⇧⌘P** pauses and resumes one. Over a recording: **Space** plays and pauses, **←** and **→** move five seconds, **⇧** with them moves ten, and **Home** and **End** jump to the ends.

**⌘R does not end a meeting, and that is deliberate.** Ending is not undoable, and ⌘R is the chord people press without thinking when they mean "reload" — nobody reaching for a refresh should be able to stop a recording that is running. Ending stays a button you have to look at. For the same reason ⌫ does not delete the recording you have selected.

macOS gets a real menu bar. View, Go and Meeting submenus, plus Settings… and Keyboard Shortcuts under Help. This is not decoration on this platform: a shortcut that is not in a menu is one a user can only find by being told about it, and the menu is where macOS has trained everyone to look.

Two keys that had quietly stopped working now work. Clicking the play button with the mouse used to leave the focus on it, so the next **Space** both activated the button and fired the shortcut — the recording toggled twice in one frame and looked like it had ignored you. And once you had clicked the scrubber, Space did nothing at all: the slider counted as somewhere you were typing, so the key was swallowed, while the slider itself had no use for it. Both are fixed, and the arrows still belong to the scrubber while it holds focus, so ← moves five seconds rather than ten.

**⌘F**, **⌘K**, **⌘[** / **⌘]** and page zoom behave exactly as they did. They are declared in the same table now instead of each owning its own listener, which is how they ended up in the sheet.

This release changes nothing on iOS or Android.
